subject: Post-demo follow-up: metering, tokens vs chars, and cache billing impact
messages:

Subject: Post-demo follow-up: metering, tokens vs chars, and cache billing impact

Hi Alex / FastCommerce team —

Great to meet you on the demo this morning. Quick recap and a few clarifying questions so we can put together a short, targeted quote and example bill for your use case.

Highlights from the call (confirm if I missed anything):
- Use case: personalized product pages + discovery prompts across mobile + web.
- Current expected volume: ~200k requests/month (you mentioned a high-variance window; please confirm typical weekday vs weekend).
- Typical lengths: prompt ~480 characters, model output ~1,200 characters (per our notes).
- Key asks: clear conversion to tokens, how caching affects billed tokens, and a target unit-economic ($/1M tokens) you want us to aim for in a proposal.

Two quick clarifying Qs so we can model this precisely:
1) How often are prompts identical (exact text) vs parameterized (e.g., same template, different SKU)? If identical, prefix-level caching can meaningfully reduce billed input tokens.
2) What's your target monthly budget range for the inference piece (ballpark is fine) so we can map to $/1M tokens?

I attached a short cheat sheet explaining token/char conversion and examples. I’ll coordinate an internal calc after your answers and send a line-item example showing spend at several $/1M token rates.

Next steps I propose:
- You reply with answers to the two Qs above and confirm the 200k/mo baseline.
- I’ll run the example economics and send a 1-page MAP + suggested SKU pricing.

Attachment: [Attachment: redwood-pricing-cheatsheet.pdf (PDF, 320KB)]

Thanks — Camila

From: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>

Subject: RE: Post-demo follow-up: metering, tokens vs chars, and cache billing impact

Camila —

Quick internal note before we send the public-facing explanation: customers often conflate three separate metering items. Suggest we give Alex a short, explicit section that maps to his questions:

1) Characters vs tokens: use a simple conversion (approx 4 characters = 1 token for English text) and show an example calculation.
2) Requests vs tokens: explain that requests is a count metric (how many calls) and tokens is the quantity billed per request (input + output).
3) Cache behavior vs billed tokens: clarify our prefix/prompt cache (when identical prompt prefix is re-used across requests, we don’t bill the cached input tokens), but generated tokens are billed for any tokens produced at runtime. Also note: local client-side caching (re-using outputs) is separate and has no server billing implications.

I drafted a 3-bullet explanation below we can paste into the external reply. Also propose we include a worked example using their numbers (I can do the calc once Alex confirms the 200k baseline).

Paste-able bullets (short):
- Token conversion: ~4 chars → 1 token; example: 1,680 chars (480 in + 1,200 out) ≈ 420 tokens per request.
- Billing: billed tokens = input tokens (unless removed by a cache hit) + generated tokens. We bill on consumed tokens, not raw characters.
- Caching: prefix cache removes identical prompt prefixes from billed input tokens when the cache is eligible; cached prefixes don’t incur input-token charges. However, tokens produced by the model at runtime are billed regardless of cache for generation.

If that reads OK I’ll slot the calc and example into Camila’s reply.

— Aditya

- Budget: we’re targeting ~USD 1,000/month for inference today but want to understand options if we scale to 2–3x.

Also — do you have any guidance on how much caching (prefix hits) typically reduces billed tokens for templated prompts? Even a conservative 20–40% hit rate estimate is useful for our planning.

Appreciate it — Alex

Subject: RE: Post-demo follow-up: metering, tokens vs chars, and cache billing impact

Alex — thanks for the quick clarifications. Below is a compact worked example and next steps. I’ll attach a one-page MAP that converts their numbers into spend at 3 price points and include expected savings from conservative caching.

Worked example (using your 200k requests/mo baseline):
- Average chars/request = 480 (in) + 1,200 (out) = 1,680 chars
- Conversion: 1 token ≈ 4 characters → 1,680 chars ≈ 420 tokens per request
- Monthly tokens = 420 tokens/request * 200,000 requests = 84,000,000 tokens (84M)

Spend at sample $/1M token rates (approx):
- $6 / 1M tokens → 84 * $6 = $504/month
- $12 / 1M tokens → 84 * $12 = $1,008/month
- $18 / 1M tokens → 84 * $18 = $1,512/month

Now caching impact (conservative estimate):
- If prefix-level cache has a 30% hit rate on input tokens, billed input tokens reduce by 30%. For your workload that primarily affects the 480-character prompt portion.
- Recompute with 30% input reduction: input tokens = (480 chars / 4) = 120 input tokens. With 30% hit → billed input tokens ≈ 84 tokens instead of 120 (saves 36 tokens per request).
- New tokens/request ≈ 420 - 36 = 384 tokens → monthly ≈ 76.8M tokens. At $12/1M that's ≈ $921/month (vs $1,008 without caching).

Key clarifications (short):
- We bill on tokens (input + output) after cache-eligible prefix de-duplication. Characters are only used for estimating tokens.
- Requests is a count of calls and is useful for engineering planning (throughput, concurrency), while tokens determine cost.
- Caching: prefix/prompt caching reduces billed input tokens for identical prefixes. Generated tokens are billed whenever the model creates tokens.

Next steps I propose:
1) I’ll attach a 1-page MAP with the three price points and two caching scenarios (0% and 30% hit) so procurement can see the delta.
2) If $12/1M tokens is within your procurement target (~$1,000/mo), we can draft a short trial agreement (30 days, consumption-based) and pre-authorize the HS-2197 deal.
3) Aditya / Monica — can we produce a quick internal quote and offer a negotiated $/1M tier for the first 3 months if they hit the 200k baseline?

Attachments: [Attachment: fastcommerce-MAP-draft.pdf (PDF, 140KB)]

I’ll follow up with the MAP and a proposed short call (15–20 min) if you’d like to walk through the numbers with procurement.

Best —
